# Documentation {#sec-documentation}
**Chapter 5 FS4R: Documentation**

Vital is thorough documentation. Documenting your choices—how data/scripts were obtained, code is setup, how data was cleaned, debugging of code was performed, which methods and tools were used, etc., etc., ensures transparency and supports both your future self and your colleagues.

**Project documentation (README, CHANGELOG, CONTRIBUTING)**

Project documentation helps users and contributors understand, use, and maintain your repository. Files are strongly recommended when publishing within the LTER-LIFE GitHub repository:

-   **README.md**: Provides an overview of the project, its purpose, and how to use it. Should include:
    -   Project objectives and description
    -   Instructions for installation and use
    -   Folder structure explanation
    -   Example commands or workflows
    -   Contact details and links to further resources
    -   References to publications, datasets, or related work (with persistent identifiers)
    -   Information about the computational environment
-   **CHANGELOG.md**: Keeps a log of changes to the project, including new features, fixes, improvements, and version numbers. Best practices:
    -   Use semantic versioning (e.g., 1.0.0) or year-based versioning (e.g., 2024.1)
    -   Clearly describe changes for each release
    -   Place the CHANGELOG in the root of the repository
    -   Follow the [Keep a Changelog style guide](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/)
-   **CONTRIBUTING.md**: Explains how others can contribute, report issues, and suggest improvements. Should address:
    -   Guidelines for submitting issues, merge/pull requests
    -   Coding standards and review process
    -   How to contact maintainers or admins
    -   Reference to the Code of Conduct
    -   Data policies (e.g., do not upload sensitive data, use mock/example data for demonstration)
    -   Any domain-specific quality assurance steps or required checks before publication
-   **LICENSE:** Describes how others may use, modify, or distribute your work. Keep in mind:
    -   Code cannot be reused if no license exists in the repository.
    -   We recommend the use of [open licenses](https://rivmnl.sharepoint.com/sites/Onderzoeks-enDataloketRIVM/SitePages/Open-Licenties.aspx) for software such as the [EULP v1.2](https://choosealicense.com/licenses/eupl-1.2/) and compatible licenses (e.g., Apache, GNU GPL or MIT), depending on the situation for reusability of the repository
    -   Check [https://choosealicense.com/](https://choosealicense.com/) or contact data stewards of NIOO, RIVM, or UvA for questions about open licenses.
-   **CITATION.cff** A machine-readable file providing citation metadata to allow others to properly reference your project in academic publications or reports. This is one way to present your metadata information:
    -   You can create the CITATION file easily using [ccfinit](https://citation-file-format.github.io/cff-initializer-javascript/#/), as explained in this video from the eScience Center: [How to create a CITATION.cff using cffinit](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zcgLIT5Qd4M).

**Code documentation (comments, docstrings, notebooks)**

Code documentation ensures that your code is understandable and reusable by others (and your future self). We recommend the following practices:

-   Comments:
    -   Use inline comments to clarify complex or non-obvious code sections.
    -   Focus on explaining why something is done a certain way, not just what is happening.
    -   Avoid redundant comments; keep them clear and concise.
-   Docstrings:
    -   For each function, script, or class, add a docstring or header comment explaining its purpose, parameters, return values, and exceptions.
    -   In R: as an example use [roxygen2](https://roxygen2.r-lib.org/) for function documentation.
    -   In Python: Follow [PEP 257 conventions](https://peps.python.org/pep-0257/) for docstrings.
-   Notebooks:
    -   Use Jupyter Notebooks (.ipynb), R Markdown (.Rmd), or Quarto for analyses, workflows, and demonstrations.
    -   Combine code, narrative, and output to make analyses transparent and reproducible.
    -   Include sufficient narrative to explain the steps, data sources, and results.
-   Examples and Tutorials:
    -   Provide example scripts, walkthroughs, or notebooks in a /docs or /examples folders.
    -   Clearly indicate where users should start.
    -   If your project includes computational environments or dependencies, reference these in the documentation so users know how to set up and run your code

**Keeping documentation up-to-date**

Documentation is only useful if it reflects the current state of the project. Make updating documentation part of your development workflow:

-   Update documentation files (README, CONTRIBUTING, CHANGELOG, etc.) whenever code, data, or project structure changes.
-   Review documentation regularly for relevance and completeness, especially before major releases or sharing the repository publicly.
-   Encourage all contributors to help maintain and improve documentation, and treat documentation changes as part of the code review process.
-   Reference documentation status and update needs in your version control workflow (for example, linking issues or merge requests to documentation tasks).

By maintaining clear, accurate, and up-to-date documentation throughout your project’s lifecycle, you ensure your work is compliant to open science standards, ready for effective collaboration, and future reuse.

**Frameworks to assess model/script quality and transparency**

In addition, there are several frameworks to assess model/script quality and transparency. Below you will find a large number of aspects that were setup by Wageningen University & Research Centre, adopted and extended by RIVM, which can be used to assess model/script quality and transparency. For each aspect, the number 1-3 represent an increase in the effort to ensure quality & transparency.

**1\. The model is described**

1.1 The goal and scope are documented

1.  The goal and intended scope are described
2.  The scope is justified by fitness for purpose
3.  The limitations of the model or script are described.

1.2 There is a general description of the model

1.  What does the model do?
2.  The theoretical framework is documented. Used paradigms are motivated and described in relation to the model’s purpose.
3.  The application of the model is justified in relation to stakeholders.

1.3 The conceptual and formal model are documented

1.  The formal model is documented.
2.  The conceptual model is documented, including assumptions, simplifications, and is embedded in literature.
3.  The model’s complexity is justified and there is a peer-reviewed scientific publication.

**2\. The technical implementation of the model is documented**

2.1 The implementation of the model is documented

1.  Reproducibility document
2.  Basic structure and/or flow diagram
3.  Justified (modular) design

2.2 The source code or script is commented (see chapter 6 for version control)

1.  Author’s name
2.  Basic comments in the code and/or comment guidelines
3.  Comments in the code with complete coverage and/or code reviews

2.3 The development environment is documented

1.  Programming language
2.  The IDE and settings are documented
3.  Limitations of the development environment are documented and there is a justified choice for the environment

2.4 The implementation is verified

1.  Verified within the core parameter domain
2.  Behavior at the extremes of the domain
3.  External verification

2.5 The implementation is tested

1.  Happy flow integration test recorded. Logbook for model development
2.  Tests documented and/or test protocol. Untested components identified.
3.  Code coverage of the tests is documented.

**3\. The parameters, variables, input and output of the model are described**

3.1 The parameters and variables of the model are documented

1.  (Inline) description and units
2.  Quantities, default values, standard source and description
3.  Range and accuracy

3.2 Calibration of parameters is described

1.  Description or repeatable scripts
2.  Procedure and results discussed
3.  Justified choice of method and discussion of alternatives

3.3 The input and output are described

1.  (Inline) description and units
2.  Structure, format, quantities, accuracy, description, linking variables and parameters and version echo
3.  (Inter)national standards and input echo & timestamp

3.4 The origin of data is described

1.  Citation or unique identifier for all sources
2.  Data preparation pipeline, data source, and scripts tested
3.  Protocol for data collection, periodically updated, duration of validity, date of last update

**4\. The functioning of the model is evaluated**

4.1 A sensitivity analysis has been performed

1.  Documented experience (logbook)
2.  Tailored to model type, documented and discussed
3.  Motivated, documented protocol and evaluated

4.2 An uncertainty analysis has been performed

1.  N.A. (may be skipped)
2.  Qualitative discussion
3.  Quantitative analysis and evaluated

4.3 The model is validated

1.  Documented ‘face validation’ (logbook)
2.  Discussed validation and non-validated components identified
3.  Motivated, documented protocol and evaluated

4.4 Use of the model is tracked

1.  N.A. (may be skipped)
2.  Example studies identified
3.  Use and user experience tracked, evaluated and documented

4.5 There is a general description of model ‘fitness for purpose’

1.  Main considerations are documented. With references to similar approach/principle/method
2.  Relation of purpose to: test, sensitivity, uncertainty, validation and use
3.  Reliability
